client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Everything just feels kind of gray and hollow — like I go through the motions of my day but nothing actually feels good or meaningful anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, honestly, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: Thank you for showing up and giving this a chance, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that kind of ambivalence is really honest and completely understandable, especially when you're carrying grief this heavy. What you're describing, that gray, hollow feeling where the days keep moving but nothing lands, sounds like a very real and painful response to losing someone who mattered deeply to you. I'm curious — when you think about your grandmother, what's the feeling that comes up most strongly for you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: When I think about her, the first thing that hits me is this wave of guilt, honestly. Like, I keep replaying the last few months before she passed and thinking about all the times I didn't visit because I was "too busy" with work or whatever excuse I had. It's hard to just feel sad about missing her because the guilt kind of takes over everything and makes it feel like I don't even deserve to grieve properly.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — the idea that you don't *deserve* to grieve — is such a painful place to be stuck, and it's also one of the most common ways grief gets complicated. I want to gently offer something to sit with: the fact that you're carrying this much guilt actually speaks to how much you loved her, not to what kind of person you were to her. Can you tell me a little about what your relationship with her was like beyond those last few months — what did she mean to you, and what do you think she saw when she looked at you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I want to believe what you're saying, that the guilt means I loved her... but it feels like a convenient thing to say, like something you'd tell anyone to make them feel better. Before those last few months, she was honestly one of the only people who really got me — she'd call just to check in, not because anything was wrong, just because she was thinking of me. But when I try to hold onto that version of us, the good years, it just gets swallowed up by the image of me not being there enough at the end.
therapist: It's fair to push back on that — you don't have to accept something just because I say it, and I'd rather earn your trust than have you take comfort that doesn't feel real. What strikes me, though, is the way you described her — someone who called just because she was thinking of you, not because anything was wrong — that's a rare and specific kind of love, and *you* were the person she chose to give it to. I'm wondering, if she were here right now and could hear the story you're telling about yourself — the one where you failed her at the end — what do you think she would actually say?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: I think she would probably tell me I'm being too hard on myself... that's what she always said when I got like this. But the thing is, she's not here to say it, and that's kind of the whole problem, isn't it? It almost makes it worse to imagine her voice saying those words, because then I just miss her more and it reminds me that I can't actually ask her.
therapist: What you just said is so achingly true — that the very thing that might comfort you also opens the wound wider, because her voice in your mind is a reminder of the silence where she used to be. There's something really significant in the fact that she knew this part of you, the part that gets too hard on yourself, and loved you through it anyway, enough that her words are still living inside you even now. I wonder if that voice — the one that says you're being too hard on yourself — is something she gave you on purpose, something she'd want you to be able to use even without her here to say it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's... a really hard thing to sit with, because part of me wants to believe that, that she left me something to carry forward. But another part of me feels like I'm just making it up, like I'm projecting meaning onto grief because it hurts less than accepting she's just gone. I don't know if I can trust that voice when it feels like it might just be me desperately holding onto her.
therapist: The tension you're naming — between meaning-making and "just making it up" — is one of the most honest things a grieving person can wrestle with, and I don't think those two things are actually opposites. Even if *you* are the one choosing to carry her voice forward, that choice itself is an act of love, not a trick you're playing on yourself. I'm curious — when she said those words to you in real life, did they feel true then, or did part of you resist them even when she was still here to say them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That's... actually a really good question, and I didn't expect it to stop me like that. Honestly, yeah, even when she was alive I sometimes brushed off what she said about me being capable, like she was just being a mom and didn't really see me clearly. So now I'm sitting here wondering if the problem isn't just that she's gone, but that I never fully let her words land even when she was here to mean them.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that this pattern of deflecting her belief in you didn't start with her death, it was already there, which means this might be less about grief and more about a longer relationship you've had with not fully letting in the people who see you clearly. And there's something almost tender in the way you're realizing this right now, like she's still managing to show you something true about yourself even from here. I'm wondering — what do you think got in the way of letting her words land back then?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think... part of me always assumed she was saying those things because she loved me, not because they were actually true. Like, love makes people see you through a filter, you know? So I'd just smile and nod and think, "she has to say that, she's my mom."
therapist: That belief — "she has to say it, so it doesn't count" — is such a quietly painful way to live, because it creates a rule where love itself becomes a reason to distrust the very people most likely to see you clearly. I notice you're speaking about this pretty quickly, like maybe it's easier to explain it as a logical system than to feel what it cost you to spend years filtering her out that way. What does it bring up for you to consider that she might have *both* loved you deeply *and* been telling the truth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... it brings up something I don't really have a word for. Like, if she actually meant it, then I've been alone in a way I didn't have to be, and that's... that's a lot to sit with. It's almost easier to keep thinking she was just being nice, because the other option means I wasted something real.
therapist: What you just said landed really quietly, but I don't think it's a small thing at all — the idea that you could have been less alone, that the connection was real and available, is genuinely grief on top of grief. I want to stay with you in that for a moment, because the way you said it — "I wasted something real" — sounds like another version of that same harsh judgment you've been turning on yourself this whole time. What if the more honest framing is that you protected yourself the only way you knew how, and that the waste, if there was any, wasn't yours alone to carry?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to feel like I was the one who kept pulling back, who made excuses not to show up. Like, maybe they were doing their part and I just... didn't meet them there. And even if you're right that I was protecting myself, it still feels like the cost of that protection was losing something I actually needed.
therapist: The way you just said that — "I actually needed" — feels like one of the most unguarded things you've shared today, like something slipped through before you could qualify it. And I notice you're still holding yourself as the one who failed, even as you're also acknowledging that what you were protecting yourself *from* was real. I want to ask you gently — what do you think you were so afraid of, back then, that made it feel safer to keep some distance from someone who loved you that much?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think... I was afraid that if I let myself fully need him, and then something happened, it would destroy me completely. Like keeping that little bit of distance was my way of making sure I'd survive if he left, or if I somehow messed it up. And I did mess it up, so maybe part of me thinks the distance didn't even work, it just made me lose him faster.
therapist: What you just described — keeping distance as a way to survive loss — is one of the most human things I've ever heard, and it makes complete sense that a younger version of you learned to do that. But I want to gently reflect something back: you've been speaking quickly, like you're racing to get through something that might be too big to slow down inside of, and I wonder if part of you already knows that what you just said is the heart of something really important. The distance wasn't a flaw in you — it was armor — but it sounds like you're finally ready to ask whether you still need to wear it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
